o: Given an n x n grid of distinct values 0..n²-1, support two queries: the sum of orthogonally adjacent neighbors of a value, and the sum of diagonally adjacent neighbors. Since n <= 10 and there are at most 2n² calls, almost anything works; the clean design is to map each value to its coordinates (or precompute both sums per value) at construction time.
k: Values are distinct and bounded by n²-1, so they can index arrays directly.
Precomputing per-value adjacent/diagonal sums makes each query O(1).
Boundary checks handle edge/corner cells with fewer neighbors.

a.i: Store value -> (row, col) in a hash map at construction. Each query looks up the coordinates and sums the in-bounds neighbors using fixed direction offsets. Constant factors are tiny given n <= 10.
s: Build pos[v] = (i, j) while scanning the grid.
adjacentSum: sum grid[ni][nj] over the four orthogonal offsets that stay in bounds.
diagonalSum: same with the four diagonal offsets.

a.i: Since values fit in [0, n²-1], precompute two flat arrays adj[v] and dia[v] during construction by iterating over all cells and adding each cell's value to its neighbors' entries. Queries become pure array reads — the fastest possible per-call behavior.
s: Allocate adj and dia arrays of size n².
For each cell, for each in-bounds orthogonal neighbor w: adj[w] += cell value; likewise for diagonals into dia.
a.sp: O(n²) for the two precomputed arrays

w: Either approach is fine at these scales; precomputation wins if query counts were enormous. Pitfall: forgetting bounds checks for border cells. Follow-up: support grid updates — then a position map with on-the-fly neighbor recomputation is the better design.
